codes.label: Total monthly cost vs. current rent
codes.definition: Compare the full monthly cost of owning (mortgage, taxes, insurance, maintenance, utilities, any HOA fees) against what the person pays in rent today, rather than looking at the mortgage payment alone.

codes.label: Pre-approval is a ceiling, not a budget
codes.definition: A lender's maximum approval reflects borrowing capacity at a moment in time, not what the person can comfortably carry, so a lower price or payment may leave a needed safety margin.

codes.label: Liquidity left after closing / emergency fund
codes.definition: After the down payment, closing costs, moving costs and repairs, check how much cash remains and whether that is enough of an emergency cushion; a thin reserve matters more than the size of the down payment.

codes.label: Illiquid home equity and opportunity cost of savings
codes.definition: Putting most savings into a home converts accessible money into an illiquid asset and forgoes what that money could earn invested or held in reserve, so weigh equity-building against flexibility.

codes.label: Down payment size, PMI and closing costs
codes.definition: A down payment under 20 percent can bring private mortgage insurance, and closing costs add several percent of the price, both of which raise the true cash and monthly cost of buying.

codes.label: Interest rate, loan type and loan term
codes.definition: The rate, fixed versus adjustable structure, lender shopping and loan length (including a 30-year term running into later life) drive the total cost and long-run affordability of the mortgage.

codes.label: Job or income loss risk and single-income stress test
codes.definition: Test whether the mortgage and essentials remain payable if an income drops or disappears for several months, especially when an employer is cutting jobs or the household relies on one salary.

codes.label: Correlated household income risk
codes.definition: If both earners are exposed to the same employer, industry or local economy, a downturn could hit both incomes at once, so the safety margin is thinner than two paychecks suggest.

codes.label: Reduced income and added costs from having a child
codes.definition: A planned child may bring parental leave, childcare, medical costs and a shift to one income, so the budget should be tested against that period rather than today's dual-income snapshot.

codes.label: Space and neighborhood fit for a growing family
codes.definition: Whether the home's size, layout, schools, childcare access and commute will suit the family's needs over the next several years, including future resale appeal.

codes.label: How long they will stay / transaction costs of selling
codes.definition: Buying and selling cost roughly 6 to 10 percent of the price, so a short holding period due to a move or changed plans can erase equity; the expected length of stay determines whether buying pays off.

codes.label: Flexibility and reversibility: renting vs. owning
codes.definition: Renting keeps the option to relocate, downsize or change plans on short notice, while owning is slow and costly to reverse and ties the person to a place, market and set of obligations.

codes.label: Value of waiting or renting longer
codes.definition: Consider delaying the purchase to build savings, see how job or life uncertainty resolves, or buy something cheaper, and weigh the cost of waiting against the cost of buying into uncertainty.

codes.label: Roof or major repair as a known near-term expense
codes.definition: A roof needing replacement within a few years is a substantial, near-certain cost whose price and timing should be quoted now and factored into the budget and the cash needed after closing.

codes.label: Using the repair issue to negotiate price or credit
codes.definition: A documented estimate for a known defect can justify a lower price, a seller credit, a holdback or seller-paid repair rather than the buyer absorbing the whole cost.

codes.label: Inspection and hidden defects
codes.definition: Beyond the known problem, a full inspection can uncover foundation, plumbing, electrical, HVAC, water or pest issues that would change what the property is really worth and what it will cost.

codes.label: Offer deadline pressure and protective contingencies
codes.definition: A short deadline and competing offers create urgency that can push a rushed decision, so decide a walk-away price in advance, ask for an extension or time for inspection, and think hard before waiving inspection, financing or appraisal protections.

codes.label: Property taxes, insurance and reassessment
codes.definition: Property tax and homeowners insurance vary by location, can rise over time, and may reset upward after a purchase, so the actual annual amounts for the specific property should be verified.

codes.label: Ongoing maintenance and upkeep burden
codes.definition: Owning brings recurring repair and upkeep costs and work that a renter does not face, typically budgeted at a percentage of the home's value per year, plus the physical burden of managing it as one ages.

codes.label: Condo fee stability and special assessments
codes.definition: Association fees tend to rise and can be accompanied by lump-sum special assessments, so the fee should not be treated as fixed and should be checked against the budget with escalation.

codes.label: Condo association financial health and rules
codes.definition: The reserve fund, reserve study, meeting minutes, pending litigation, insurance coverage and rules on rentals, pets and governance indicate whether the building's finances and community are sound.

codes.label: Resale value and local market conditions
codes.definition: Whether prices in the area are likely to rise, hold or fall, whether the purchase price is fair against comparables, and how easily the property could be sold or rented out later.

codes.label: Tax implications of buying vs. renting
codes.definition: Mortgage interest and property tax deductions, the effect of the standard deduction, and capital gains rules on a future sale change the real after-tax cost of owning and should be modeled rather than assumed.

codes.label: Retirement timeline and ability to keep saving
codes.definition: With a fixed number of working years left, test whether the purchase still leaves room to keep contributing to retirement and reach the target retirement age.

codes.label: Housing costs on a fixed retirement income
codes.definition: Consider whether a mortgage, fees and taxes would still be affordable once salary is replaced by Social Security, pension and savings withdrawals, versus rent that could keep rising.

codes.label: Retirement income sources
codes.definition: Get a clear picture of projected Social Security timing and benefits, any pension, retirement account balances, healthcare costs and any divorce-related benefits to see how much retirement income can be relied on.

codes.label: Sequence-of-returns and market-downturn risk near retirement
codes.definition: Draining savings into one illiquid asset just before retirement increases exposure if markets fall or a forced sale or borrowing is needed in the years around retiring.

codes.label: Concentration of net worth in one asset
codes.definition: Committing a large share of total wealth to a single property changes the person's overall risk profile and leaves less in diversified, accessible holdings.

codes.label: Favorable existing tenancy and lease terms
codes.definition: A long, stable rental with a below-market, predictable rent is a valuable arrangement already working, and giving it up should be priced into the comparison; lease notice terms also affect move timing.

codes.label: Non-financial value of stability, control and identity
codes.definition: Ownership can bring a sense of stability, control over one's space and having built something, or can feel like a burdensome responsibility and lock-in, and these personal feelings deserve weight alongside the numbers.

codes.label: Moving closer to family as a separate decision
codes.definition: A request to relocate near a relative is its own question, and a purchase in the current city could make a later move harder, so separate whether to move from whether to buy.

codes.label: Value of proximity to family and future care support
codes.definition: Living near family offers companionship and informal support as one ages, which may reduce paid care needs, and it depends on whether that relative actually wants and can sustain the arrangement.

codes.label: Cost and consequences of relocating to a different market
codes.definition: Moving across the country involves job change, loss of community, new local housing prices and possible effects on pension service credit or insurance, so costs should be evaluated for the new location rather than assumed to match the current one.

codes.label: Aging in place: accessibility, health and care needs
codes.definition: Consider whether the home's stairs, elevator reliability, layout and modification costs, and proximity to doctors and services will support future mobility and care needs.

codes.label: Community and social ties
codes.definition: Existing routines, friends, services, job and neighborhood connections have real quality-of-life value that a move would disrupt.

codes.label: Divorce-related financial obligations and documents
codes.definition: Settlement terms, retirement account divisions, support obligations, beneficiary designations and estate documents affect how much can safely be committed and how the asset would pass on.

codes.label: Insurance coverage for income interruption
codes.definition: Life, disability and long-term care coverage determine whether a mortgage would become a burden if income were interrupted by illness, injury or death.

codes.label: Income and borrowing qualification
codes.definition: Whether salary, credit score and debt-to-income ratio support a mortgage on reasonable terms, including how lenders treat job changes before closing.

codes.label: Possible changes in household composition
codes.definition: A future change such as remarriage or other shifts in who lives in the home could alter housing needs, finances and the property's suitability.

codes.label: Professional advice and scenario modeling
codes.definition: Consulting a fee-only financial planner or housing counselor to model buy-versus-rent break-even, cash flow, taxes and retirement scenarios side by side before committing.

codes.label: Eligibility for buyer or senior programs and benefits
codes.definition: Check whether any first-time buyer, downsizing or senior-related programs or tax benefits could reduce the cost of purchasing.
